title: Complexity and Big O
summary: A plain-language way to compare how algorithms grow, so you can choose an approach before you write it.
keyPoints: Big O describes how work grows as the input grows, not how many milliseconds a specific machine takes.
Drop constant factors and lower-order terms because they stop mattering at large input sizes.
A loop over n items is O(n); a loop inside another loop over n items is usually O(n²).
Space complexity counts extra memory you allocate, not the input itself.

complexity.note: The table itself uses linear memory.
The search range halves each step.
Memory can grow if you store results.
Merge sort is the usual example.
Each item is either in or out.

commonMistakes: Looking only at the loop count and ignoring what happens inside the loop, such as a sort or a full array copy.
Saying an algorithm is O(n) because it ran quickly on one small test.
Forgetting that recursion and the call stack also use space.
interviewNotes: Say the complexity out loud before coding and again after coding. Interviewers listen for whether you can revise your estimate.
Name the dominant term only: O(n² + n) becomes O(n²). Mention constants separately if they matter for the actual limits.
If the input is tiny, a simple O(n²) solution can be the right engineering choice. State that trade-off instead of hiding it.

checkYourself.question: Why is a single loop that does three operations per item still O(n)?
checkYourself.answer: The three operations are constant work per item. Constant factors are dropped, so the growth is linear.

checkYourself.question: What is the difference between time and space complexity?
checkYourself.answer: Time complexity counts how the number of steps grows. Space complexity counts how extra memory grows. Both describe growth, not exact seconds or bytes.

checkYourself.question: A function scans the array, then scans it again. What is the complexity?
checkYourself.answer: O(n). Two separate passes are O(2n), and constant factors are dropped.
